title: Book IV: Three Love Problems — Chapter XXXVI
paragraphs:
’T is strange to see the humors of these men,
These great aspiring spirits, that should be wise:
. . . . . . . .
For being the nature of great spirits to love
To be where they may be most eminent;
They, rating of themselves so farre above
Us in conceit, with whom they do frequent,
Imagine how we wonder and esteeme
All that they do or say; which makes them strive
To make our admiration more extreme,
Which they suppose they cannot, ’less they give
Notice of their extreme and highest thoughts.
—DANIEL: _Tragedy of Philotas_.

Mr. Vincy came home from hearing the will with his views on many subjects considerably altered. He was a man open to impressions, but inclined to express himself indirectly. A disappointing market for his silk braids made him swear at the groom; annoyance with his brother-in-law Bulstrode produced cutting observations on Methodism. His newly stern view of Fred's idleness now became apparent when he flung an embroidered cap out of the smoking room onto the hall floor.
“Well, sir,” he remarked as Fred headed for bed, “I hope you've decided to return next term and pass your examination. I've made up my mind, and I advise you not to waste time making up yours.”

Fred said nothing. He was too completely crushed. Twenty-four hours earlier, he had expected that by now he would no longer need to consider what to do: he would know that he need do nothing. He would hunt in a scarlet coat, own a first-rate hunter, ride to the meet on a fine hack, and earn general respect for it all. He would also repay Mr. Garth immediately, and Mary could have no further reason to refuse him. All this was supposed to happen without studying or any other inconvenience, through Providence's kindness as embodied in an old gentleman's whim. Now, at the end of those twenty-four hours, every confident expectation lay overturned. It seemed “rather hard lines” to be treated, while still smarting with disappointment, as though he could have prevented it. But he left without speaking, and his mother took his part.

“Don't treat the poor boy harshly, Vincy. He'll do well yet, although that wicked man deceived him. As surely as I'm sitting here, Fred will turn out well. Why else was he saved from the edge of the grave? I call it robbery. Promising him the land was as good as giving it. And what counts as a promise if making everybody believe you doesn't? Besides, he actually left him ten thousand pounds and then withdrew it.”
“Withdrew it!” Mr. Vincy repeated irritably. “The boy brings bad luck, Lucy, that's what I say. And you've always indulged him.”
“He was my first, Vincy. You made quite a fuss over him yourself when he arrived. Nobody could have been prouder,” said Mrs. Vincy, readily regaining her cheerful smile.
“Who can tell what a baby will grow into? No doubt I behaved like a fool,” her husband said, though his voice had softened.

“But whose children are handsomer or better than ours? Fred is miles ahead of other people's sons. You can hear in the way he speaks that he's mixed with university men. And where would you find another girl like Rosamond? Put her beside the grandest lady in the country and the comparison would only flatter her. Look at Mr. Lydgate. He's been everywhere and mixed with the best society, and he fell in love with her straightaway. Not that I wouldn't have preferred Rosamond to wait before getting engaged. On a visit she might have met someone who'd have been a much better match—I mean visiting her schoolfriend Miss Willoughby. That family has relations every bit as grand as Mr. Lydgate's.”
“Damn their relations!” exclaimed Mr. Vincy. “I've had my fill of relations. I don't want a son-in-law whose only recommendation is his family.”

“But, my dear,” Mrs. Vincy replied, “you seemed perfectly delighted. I wasn't home, admittedly, but Rosamond said you'd raised no objection whatever to the engagement. She's already started buying the finest linen and cambric for her underclothes.”

“Not with my approval,” said Mr. Vincy. “I've enough on my hands this year with an idle rascal for a son, without buying wedding clothes as well. Money couldn't be tighter; everyone's being ruined. I doubt Lydgate possesses a farthing. I won't consent to the wedding. They can wait, as their elders did before them.”
“Rosamond will be very upset, Vincy. You know you've never been able to bear refusing her.”
“Yes, I have. The sooner they break it off, the better. At this rate he'll never earn a living. All I hear of him making is enemies.”
“But Mr. Bulstrode thinks very highly of him, my dear. I'd expect the marriage to please _him_.”

“The devil it would!” said Mr. Vincy. “Bulstrode won't support them. If Lydgate imagines I'm providing money to set up their house, he's mistaken. That's all. I shall probably have to give up my horses soon. You'd better pass that on to Rosy.”

Mr. Vincy often followed this course: agree rashly in a jovial mood, then, on realizing his rashness, get someone else to perform the unpleasant retraction. Mrs. Vincy, never willingly opposing her husband, told Rosamond what he had said first thing next morning. Rosamond listened silently while examining some worked muslin. At the end she turned her graceful neck in a particular way which only long acquaintance would have taught you signified absolute obstinacy.
“What do you think, darling?” her mother asked with affectionate respect.

“Papa means no such thing,” Rosamond answered with complete composure. “He has always wanted me to marry the man I love. I intend to marry Mr. Lydgate. Papa gave his consent seven weeks ago. And I hope we'll take Mrs. Bretton's house.”

“Well, my dear, I'll leave your papa to you. You always manage everyone. But whenever we buy the damask, we must go to Sadler's—much better than Hopkins's. Mrs. Bretton's house is very big, though. I'd love you to have it, but furnishing it will be expensive: carpets and everything else, besides silver and glass. And you've heard your papa says he'll give no money. Do you suppose Mr. Lydgate is counting on any?”
“Surely you don't imagine I could ask him, Mamma. Naturally he knows his own circumstances.”

“He may have expected money, though, my dear. We all thought you'd receive a nice legacy too, besides Fred's. Now everything is so dreadful. There's no pleasure in thinking about anything, with that poor boy so disappointed.”

“That doesn't concern my marriage, Mamma. Fred needs to stop being idle. I'm taking this upstairs to Miss Morgan; she's very good at open hemming. Mary Garth could do some sewing for me now, I should think. Her needlework is exquisite—it's the nicest thing about her. I'd love double hems on all my cambric frills, and they take such a long time.”

Mrs. Vincy was right to trust Rosamond's ability to manage her father. For all his bluster, Mr. Vincy got his own way outside his dinners and his coursing about as rarely as a prime minister. Circumstances easily overpowered him, as they do most pleasure-loving, red-faced men. The circumstance called Rosamond was especially powerful, thanks to that gentle persistence which, as we know, lets a soft white living thing force its way through opposing rock. Papa was no rock. His only consistency lay in recurring changes of impulse, sometimes called habit. These gave him little chance of taking the one decisive course over his daughter's engagement: investigating Lydgate's finances thoroughly, declaring that he himself could provide no money, and forbidding either a hasty wedding or an engagement that would have to last too long. Written down, that sounds simple and easy. But an unpleasant resolution formed in the cold morning had as many enemies as an early frost and rarely survived the day's warming influences. Even Mr. Vincy's usual indirect but emphatic ways of expressing disapproval were much restricted here. Lydgate's pride made insinuations plainly dangerous, and throwing his hat on the floor was impossible. Mr. Vincy was slightly awed by him; slightly vain that he wanted Rosamond; slightly reluctant to discuss money, since his own position was weak; slightly afraid of losing an argument to a better-educated, better-bred man; and slightly afraid of displeasing his daughter. The role he preferred was generous host, beyond criticism. Business prevented any formal announcement of opposition during the first half of the day. Dinner, wine, whist, and general contentment prevented it during the second. Meanwhile each passing hour left its little deposit, gradually building the final reason for inaction: it was too late to act. The accepted suitor spent most evenings at Lowick Gate. Under Mr. Vincy's eyes, courtship flourished without depending in the least on advances from fathers-in-law or anticipated professional earnings. Young love spins such a delicate web! Even its anchors, the things from which its fine threads hang, are barely visible: fingertips briefly touching, glances meeting from blue and dark eyes, unfinished sentences, tiny movements of cheek and lip, the faintest tremors. The web itself consists of beliefs that arise unbidden, indefinable joys, one life reaching toward another, visions of wholeness, limitless trust. Lydgate spun it out of himself at astonishing speed, despite experience supposedly completed by the drama of Laure, and despite medicine and biology too. Examining softened muscle, or eyes displayed on a dish like Santa Lucia's, and other incidents of scientific research appear less incompatible with poetic love than natural dullness or a lively devotion to the coarsest prose of life. Rosamond, meanwhile, was like a water lily opening in amazement at its own fuller existence. She, too, worked busily at their shared web. This all happened in the drawing-room corner by the piano. However fine its threads, the light turned them into a rainbow visible to many besides Mr. Farebrother. Without a formal announcement, everyone in Middlemarch became certain that Miss Vincy and Mr. Lydgate were engaged.
Aunt Bulstrode grew anxious again. This time she approached her brother, deliberately visiting him at the warehouse to avoid Mrs. Vincy's changeableness. His answers did not reassure her.

“Walter, surely you haven't let all this proceed without investigating Mr. Lydgate's prospects?” Mrs. Bulstrode's eyes widened solemnly as she looked at her brother, in his irritable warehouse mood. “Think how this girl has been raised—in luxury and, I'm sorry to say, far too much worldliness. How will she manage on little money?”

“Confound it, Harriet! What am I to do when men settle here without being asked by me? Did you close your door to Lydgate? Nobody has promoted him more than Bulstrode. I never made a fuss over the fellow. Go and discuss it with your husband instead of me.”
“Really, Walter, how can this be Mr. Bulstrode's fault? He certainly never wanted the engagement.”
“If Bulstrode hadn't supported him, I would never have invited him.”
“But you brought him in to treat Fred, and that surely was a mercy,” Mrs. Bulstrode said, losing her way in the argument's complications.

“Mercy, I don't know,” said Mr. Vincy sharply. “What I know is my family causes me more worry than I care for. I was a good brother to you before you married Bulstrode, Harriet. He doesn't always show your family the friendliness one might reasonably expect.” Mr. Vincy resembled a Jesuit very little, yet the most skillful Jesuit could scarcely have redirected a question more neatly. Harriet now had to defend her husband instead of reproaching her brother. The conversation wandered so far from its starting point that it ended with a recent clash between the brothers-in-law at a parish meeting.

Mrs. Bulstrode kept her brother's complaints from her husband, but that evening she mentioned Rosamond and Lydgate. He did not share her affectionate concern. He spoke only with resignation about the hazards of starting a medical practice and the need for caution.
“Surely we ought to pray for that thoughtless girl, brought up as she has been,” Mrs. Bulstrode said, hoping to stir his feelings.

“Indeed, my dear,” Mr. Bulstrode agreed. “Those who do not belong to this world can do little else to check the mistakes of people stubbornly devoted to it. We must learn to accept that where your brother's family is concerned. I should have preferred Mr. Lydgate not to make such a marriage. But my association with him extends only to employing his abilities for God's purposes, in accordance with the example of divine government under every dispensation.”

Mrs. Bulstrode let the matter drop. She attributed her slight dissatisfaction to her own deficient spirituality. She believed her husband belonged among the men whose memoirs ought to be written after their deaths.

Lydgate himself, once accepted, was ready to accept every consequence, all of which he believed he could foresee perfectly. Naturally he must marry within a year—perhaps six months. He had not planned this, but his other plans would not be obstructed: they would merely rearrange themselves. Marriage naturally called for the usual preparations. He would need a house instead of his present rooms. Having heard Rosamond admire old Mrs. Bretton's house in Lowick Gate, he noticed when her death left it empty and immediately began negotiating for it.

He did this as a minor matter, much as he ordered everything necessary for perfect dress from his tailor, without imagining he was extravagant. Indeed, he would have despised a display of expense. His work had acquainted him with every degree of poverty, and he felt deeply for those suffering hardship. He would have behaved impeccably at a table where sauce came in a jug with a broken handle. Of a grand dinner, he might remember only a man who had talked well. Yet it had never occurred to him to live otherwise than in what he would have called the ordinary way, with green glasses for hock and excellent service at meals. He had warmed himself at French social theories without carrying away any scent of singeing. We can handle even the most radical opinions unharmed while our furniture, dinner parties, and preference for a personal coat of arms bind us inseparably to the established order. Lydgate did not, in any case, incline toward radical opinions. Particular about his boots, he would have disliked barefoot doctrines. Only in medical reform and the pursuit of discovery was he radical. Elsewhere in practical life he followed inherited habits, partly from the personal pride and unthinking self-centeredness I have already called commonness, partly from the innocence that comes of absorption in favorite ideas.

When Lydgate privately considered the consequences of the engagement that had crept up on him, he worried about too little time, not too little money. Being in love, and constantly expected by someone who always proved prettier than memory could make her, certainly interfered with diligent use of spare hours. Some “plodding German fellow” might use those hours to make the great discovery now so close at hand. This was actually an argument against postponing marriage too long, as Lydgate suggested one day to Mr. Farebrother. The Vicar had brought some pond specimens to examine under a better microscope than his own. Finding Lydgate's table of instruments and specimens in disorder, he remarked sarcastically—
“Eros has gone downhill. He began by bringing order and harmony; now he's restoring chaos.”
“At certain stages, yes,” said Lydgate, smiling and raising his eyebrows as he adjusted the microscope. “A better order follows afterward.”
“Before long?” the Vicar asked.

“I certainly hope so. This unsettled situation eats up time, and for a man with scientific ideas, every moment offers a chance. I'm convinced marriage is best for anyone wanting to work consistently. Then everything is at home. No distracting questions about his personal future; he can have peace and freedom.”
“Lucky devil,” said the Vicar, “to have all that ahead of you—Rosamond, peace, and freedom, all yours. And here I am with only a pipe and microscopic pond creatures. Well, are you ready?”

Lydgate did not tell the Vicar his other reason for wanting a shorter courtship. Even with love intoxicating him, it irritated him to spend so much time among the Vincys, obliged to join in Middlemarch gossip, lengthy festivities, whist, and general pointlessness. He had to listen respectfully when Mr. Vincy settled questions with decisive ignorance, especially the question of which drinks best pickled one's insides against unhealthy air. Mrs. Vincy's simple openness carried no suspicion that she might subtly offend her prospective son-in-law's taste. Altogether, Lydgate had to admit he was marrying slightly beneath him in Rosamond's family. But that exquisite creature suffered in much the same way herself. At least he could take pleasure in knowing that marriage to him would give her a much-needed change of soil.
“Darling!” he said one evening, very gently, sitting beside her and studying her face—

First, however, I must mention that he had found her alone in the drawing room. The great old-fashioned window, nearly as wide as the room, stood open to the summer fragrance from the back garden. Her parents had gone to a party; everyone else was outside with the butterflies.
“Darling, your eyes are red.”
“Are they?” Rosamond replied. “I wonder what caused that.” She was not one to pour out complaints or wishes. Those emerged gracefully only when invited.
“You can't hide it from me,” Lydgate said, tenderly covering both her hands with his. “Isn't there a little tear on that eyelash? Something upsets you, and you keep it from me. That's not loving.”
“Why tell you things you can't change? They're ordinary everyday troubles. Perhaps they've been a little worse recently.”
“Trouble with your family. Don't hesitate to tell me. I can guess.”

“Papa has been particularly irritable. Fred angers him. They had another quarrel this morning, because Fred threatens to waste his entire education and take up something quite beneath him. And then there's—”

Rosamond paused, her cheeks beginning to color. Lydgate had not seen her distressed since the morning they became engaged. Never had he felt more passionately for her than now. He gently kissed her hesitant lips as if to help them speak.
“I think Papa isn't entirely pleased with our engagement,” Rosamond went on, almost whispering. “Last night he said he'd certainly speak to you and insist on its being broken off.”
“Would you break it off?” Lydgate demanded, suddenly forceful, almost angry.
“I never abandon anything I've decided to do,” Rosamond replied. Touching this subject restored her composure.
“God bless you!” Lydgate kissed her again. Such firmness of purpose, properly directed, was adorable. He continued—
“Your father's too late to insist we give each other up. You're of age, and I claim you. If anyone makes you unhappy, that only gives us a reason to marry sooner.”

The blue eyes meeting his glowed with unmistakable joy. Their radiance seemed to bathe his entire future in gentle sunshine. Perfect happiness appeared to be only a few weeks away, more or less: the sort known in the Arabian Nights, when one steps out of a street's labor and quarrels into a paradise where everything is bestowed and nothing demanded.
“Why wait?” he urged passionately. “I've taken the house. We can soon arrange everything else, can't we? You won't worry about new clothes. We can buy those later.”

“You clever men do have extraordinary ideas!” Rosamond's dimples deepened as she laughed more freely than usual at this comical reversal. “I've never heard of buying wedding clothes after the wedding.”

“Surely you wouldn't make me wait months just for clothes?” said Lydgate. He half believed she was playfully tormenting him, and half feared she truly hesitated to marry soon. “Think what greater happiness we have ahead, even compared with this: always together, free of other people, arranging our lives to suit ourselves. Tell me, darling, how soon can you belong to me altogether?”

His appeal was serious, as though any fanciful delay would do him an injury. Rosamond grew serious too, and thoughtful. In fact, she was working through the complications of lace edging, stockings, and petticoat tucks in order to offer an approximate answer.
“Six weeks would be plenty. Say it would, Rosamond,” Lydgate urged, releasing her hands and gently putting an arm around her.
One small hand immediately rose to smooth her hair. She tilted her neck thoughtfully, then said in a serious tone—
“We'd need to arrange the household linen and furniture. Still, Mamma could supervise those while we're away.”
“Certainly. We must take a week or so away.”

“Oh, longer than that!” Rosamond said earnestly. She was thinking about evening dresses for visiting Sir Godwin Lydgate. For a long time she had secretly hoped to spend at least a delightful quarter of her honeymoon there, even if she postponed meeting the uncle who was a doctor of divinity—a pleasing, though quieter, distinction too, when supported by good birth. Her look expressed wondering protest. Lydgate readily assumed she wished to prolong their sweet solitude together.
“Anything you wish, darling, once we've settled the date. But let's make a firm decision and end whatever unhappiness you're experiencing. Six weeks! I'm certain that's enough.”

“I could certainly hurry the sewing,” Rosamond replied. “Then will you speak to Papa? Writing to him might be better.” She blushed and looked at him as garden flowers seem to look at us when we walk happily among them in the surpassing evening light. Is there not a soul beyond words, half child, half nymph, in those delicate petals glowing and breathing around their deeply colored centers?

His lips brushed her ear and the little curve of neck beneath it. They sat motionless for many minutes, which flowed past like a softly bubbling stream kissed by sunlight. Rosamond believed nobody could be more in love. Lydgate believed that, after all his reckless mistakes and ridiculous gullibility, he had found perfect womanhood. He could almost feel already the exquisite marital affection of an accomplished creature who revered his lofty thinking and important work and would never disturb them. Quietly, as if by magic, she would keep the house and accounts in order, yet always have her fingers ready for the lute, transforming life into romance at a touch. Her education reached exactly the proper feminine boundary, not a hair beyond it. Therefore she would be compliant and ready to obey instructions reaching her from that boundary. More than ever he saw that his plan to remain a bachelor much longer had been mistaken. Marriage would help rather than hinder him. The next day, accompanying a patient to Brassing, he happened to see a dinner service that seemed exactly right and bought it on the spot. Attending to such things when they occurred to you saved time, and he hated ugly crockery. The service was costly, but perhaps that was simply the nature of dinner services. Furnishing a home inevitably cost money; still, it needed doing only once.
“It sounds lovely,” Mrs. Vincy said when Lydgate described his purchase. “Exactly what Rosy should have. Heaven grant it doesn't get broken!”

“One must engage servants who don't break things,” Lydgate replied. Certainly his reasoning rested on an incomplete view of consequences. But at that time scarcely any kind of reasoning lacked some endorsement from scientific men.

There was naturally no need to delay telling Mamma anything. She rarely adopted an unhappy view, and, being happily married herself, felt almost nothing but pride at her daughter's marriage. Rosamond nevertheless had sound reasons for advising Lydgate to approach Papa in writing. To prepare him for the letter, she walked with him to the warehouse next morning and told him on the way that Mr. Lydgate wanted an early wedding.

“Nonsense, darling!” Mr. Vincy replied. “What money has he to marry on? You'd be far better off ending the engagement. I've already told you that plainly enough. Why give you such an education if you're going to marry a poor man? It's cruel for a father to witness.”
“He isn't poor, Papa. He purchased Mr. Peacock's practice, which is said to bring in eight or nine hundred a year.”
“Rubbish! What does buying a practice amount to? He might as well purchase next year's swallows. It'll slide straight through his hands.”
“Quite the reverse, Papa. He'll expand it. Look how the Chettams and Casaubons have called him in.”
“I hope he understands he'll get nothing from me. After this disappointment over Fred, and with Parliament about to be dissolved, machines being smashed everywhere, an election approaching—”
“Dear Papa, how does any of that concern my wedding?”

“A great deal! We could all be ruined, for all I know, with the country in this condition. People call it the end of the world; be hanged if it doesn't look like it! Anyway, this is no time to take money out of my business. I'd like Lydgate to understand that.”
“I'm certain he expects nothing, Papa. His connections are so distinguished that he's bound to advance somehow. He's working on scientific discoveries.”
Her father said nothing.

“I can't abandon my one chance of happiness, Papa. Mr. Lydgate is a gentleman. I could never love anyone who wasn't a gentleman in every way. You wouldn't want me to fall into a decline, as Arabella Hawley did. Besides, you know I never alter my decisions.”
Still her father did not answer.
“Promise you'll agree to our wishes, Papa. We'll never give each other up, and you've always disapproved of long engagements and marrying late.”
After a little more coaxing in this vein, Mr. Vincy said, “Well, well, child. He must write to me before I can reply.” Rosamond knew she had won.

Mr. Vincy's reply chiefly required Lydgate to insure his life, which he immediately agreed to do. The idea was wonderfully reassuring if Lydgate died, though meanwhile it supplied no means of living. Nevertheless, it seemed to settle everyone's anxieties about Rosamond's wedding. The necessary shopping went ahead enthusiastically, but not without due economy. A bride intending to visit a baronet must possess a few superb handkerchiefs. Beyond the six absolutely indispensable ones, however, Rosamond was content with something less than the finest embroidery and Valenciennes lace. Lydgate, too, discovering how much his eight hundred pounds had shrunk since his arrival in Middlemarch, resisted some old-pattern silver shown to him at Kibble's in Brassing, where he went for forks and spoons. He was too proud to behave as if he expected Mr. Vincy to advance money for furniture. Everything need not be paid for immediately, so some bills would remain outstanding; but he wasted no time guessing what dowry his father-in-law might provide to help settle them. He intended no extravagance. Necessary things had to be purchased, and buying inferior quality would be false economy. Such matters were incidental. He expected science and his profession to be the sole objects of his passionate effort, but could not imagine pursuing them in a home like Wrench's, with every door open, worn oilcloth, children in dirty pinafores, and lunch lingering as bones, black-handled knives, and willow-pattern plates. Then again, Wrench had a miserable, sluggish wife who wrapped herself indoors like a mummy in a large shawl. His domestic arrangements must have been badly chosen from the start.
Rosamond, for her part, did plenty of speculating, although her quick ability to perceive and imitate proper behavior warned her not to reveal it too bluntly.
“I'd so love to meet your family,” she said one day as they discussed the wedding journey. “Perhaps we could choose a route that lets us visit them on the way home. Which uncle is your favorite?”
“Oh, Godwin, I suppose. He's a kindly old fellow.”
“You spent a great deal of time at his house in Quallingham as a boy, didn't you? I'd love to see the place and everything you knew then. Have you told him you're getting married?”
“No,” Lydgate answered casually, turning in his chair and rumpling his hair.

“Then tell him, you naughty, neglectful nephew. Perhaps he'll invite you to bring me to Quallingham. You could show me the grounds, and I could picture you there as a boy. Remember, you see my home exactly as it's been since my childhood. It isn't fair that I know so little of yours. Unless perhaps you'd be a little ashamed of me—I hadn't thought of that.”

Lydgate smiled tenderly. He genuinely accepted her suggestion that the proud delight of displaying such a charming bride merited a little effort. Now that he considered it, he would enjoy revisiting the old places with Rosamond.
“All right, I'll write. My cousins are dreadful bores, though.”
To Rosamond, the ability to dismiss a baronet's family so lightly seemed magnificent. She felt very satisfied at the prospect of judging them contemptuously for herself.
A day or two later, however, Mamma nearly spoiled everything by remarking—
“I do hope your uncle Sir Godwin won't think Rosy beneath him, Mr. Lydgate. I should expect a handsome present from him. A thousand or two must be nothing to a baronet.”

“Mamma!” Rosamond blushed deeply. Lydgate felt so sorry for her that he said nothing and went to the far end of the room to study a print with apparent absorption, as if his attention had wandered. Mamma received a little lecture from her daughter afterward and was as compliant as usual. Rosamond reflected, however, that any visit to Middlemarch by those tiresome, well-born cousins would expose them to much in her own family that might shock them. It therefore seemed desirable for Lydgate eventually to secure a distinguished position somewhere else. Surely that would not be difficult for a man who could make discoveries and had a titled uncle. Lydgate, you see, had spoken ardently to Rosamond about his hopes for the highest purposes of his life. He had delighted in being heard by a creature who would support him with the sweetness of satisfying affection, beauty, and rest—the kind of help our thoughts receive from a summer sky and meadows bordered with flowers.

Lydgate put great faith in the psychological distinction between what, for variety's sake, I shall call goose and gander. Above all, he trusted the goose's inborn submissiveness to complement so beautifully the gander's strength.
